title: Band edges, ships and low-band power
blurb: Check that a sideband signal stays inside the band, and know the rules for 60 m, 630 m, 2200 m, vessels and forwarding.

E1A01.why: USB spreads **above** the carrier: 14.348 + 0.003 = 14.351 MHz, so the top 1 kHz is past the 14.350 edge.
E1A01.trap: The carrier itself is inside the band; it is the sideband that spills over.

E1A02.why: LSB spreads **below** the carrier, so the carrier must be at least one signal width (**3 kHz**) above the lower edge.
E1A02.trap: At the exact edge, the whole sideband lands outside the band.

E1A03.why: USB data grows upward and the segment ends at 14.150 MHz: 14.150 minus 0.0028 = **14.1472 MHz**. Any higher and the top spills over.

E1A04.why: LSB at 3.601 MHz extends down to about 3.598, **below the phone segment edge**. The dial reading looks legal but the sideband is not.
E1A04.trap: The displayed (carrier) frequency being inside the band is not enough.

E1A05.why: Any person with an **FCC amateur license** (or alien reciprocal authorization) may control the station. No marine license or special permit.

E1A06.why: On channelized 60 m a CW signal goes at the **centre frequency** of the channel.

E1A07.why: The 2200 m limit is **1 W EIRP**: power as radiated by the antenna, gain included, not PEP at the transmitter.
E1A07.trap: 5 W EIRP is the 630 m limit.

E1A08.why: The **control operator of the originating station** is primarily accountable. Relaying stations are not primarily accountable.

E1A09.why: The 630 m limit is **5 W EIRP** (except some parts of Alaska).
E1A09.trap: 1 W EIRP is the 2200 m limit.

E1A10.why: The **master of the ship or pilot in command** must approve before you operate.

E1A11.why: Any **FCC-issued amateur license** is enough, even on international waters. No endorsement or extra permit.
